done.why: Reached the Cerberus Room beyond the baseball maze. The three-headed dog refused every gift I tried (necklace, club, brick), and I had no idea what it wanted.

about: A Zork-like underground treasure hunt. A wizard says the treasures lie south of the ravine. Getting there means crossing a spinning carousel room, answering a riddle at a stone door, and finding the right route through a baseball-diamond glass maze.

ending.what: No ending. I took the pearl necklace and opened the secret passage under the maze. It led to the Cerberus Room and a dog I could not get past.

moments.note: The Wizard's speech told me where to go: the pearls behind a stone door that asks a question, and a room that will not keep still.
The gold ingot was an illusion from the Wizard's Fantasize spell. The text played it as a joke.
The carousel sends you to a random passage whatever direction you type. Finding the Riddle Room and Menhir Room took many tries.
Answering 'well' made the stone door open with a clap of thunder.
The glass maze's feedback was hard to read. Some steps gave 'woken', some 'lost count', and a few said there was no way.
I traced the route southeast, southeast, northeast, northwest, then southwest, and heard the rusty squeal of something opening.
Cerberus rejected everything I offered, and I had no clue what it wanted.

wished: A clearer way to pick a passage in the carousel room
Some hint about what Cerberus wants
A way to stop the carousel

lines.line: It is all south of the ravine, his look says, every treasure the Empire mislaid, and much good may it do you; the pearls nearest, behind a stone door that asks a question
lines.why: It gave me a clear goal and a route.
The deadpan reply to examining the floor.

fun.why: The riddle and the base-running puzzle paid off well. The random carousel and the unclear maze feedback dragged.

engagement.why: The Wizard's hints gave me a purpose, and each puzzle led on to the next.

difficulty.why: The carousel's randomness and the maze's cryptic feedback made progress slow, and I never worked out what the dog wanted.

interestingness.why: The Zork-flavoured setting has several distinct puzzle areas, and the Wizard's illusions and freezing add surprises.

prose.why: The prose is witty and responsive to what the player does.
